interviewQuestions.question: Define a language model in one sentence you'd actually say in an interview.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd say: "A language model is a system that assigns a probability distribution over the next token given the preceding tokens, and everything else — chat, summarization, code generation — is built on repeatedly sampling from that distribution." I'd follow with why this simple framing matters in practice: it explains why LLMs can hallucinate fluently (they're optimizing for plausible continuations, not verified truth), why prompt engineering works (you're steering the conditioning context that the probability distribution is computed from), and why scale unlocked new capabilities (a big enough model trained on enough text implicitly learns grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns as a side effect of getting next-token prediction right). I'd keep the one-sentence definition tight and precise rather than reaching for a longer, vaguer description like "an AI that understands language" — that phrasing invites follow-up questions I can't crisply answer, whereas the probability-distribution framing is exactly correct and sets up the rest of the conversation well.

**Testing:** whether you can give a precise, technically correct definition on demand rather than a marketing-style paraphrase — this is often an opening question used to calibrate how rigorous the rest of the interview should be.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: A precise one-line definition

interviewQuestions.question: Why do n-gram language models break down as n increases, and why doesn't just collecting more training text fully fix it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
N-gram models estimate P(word | previous n-1 words) purely by counting how often that exact sequence appeared in training text, divided by the count of the preceding shorter sequence. The problem is combinatorial: the number of possible n-grams grows exponentially with n and vocabulary size, so as n increases past 2 or 3, the overwhelming majority of possible n-grams — including many perfectly reasonable, grammatical ones — simply never appear in even a very large training corpus. When a specific 4-gram was never observed, its counted probability is exactly zero, regardless of whether it's a completely natural phrase a human would say without hesitation. This is the sparsity problem, and it's not a bug in the counting method — it's a structural consequence of language having combinatorially many valid sequences relative to any finite corpus.

More training text helps somewhat but can't close this gap fundamentally, because the space of possible n-grams grows faster than any realistic corpus size can cover — doubling your corpus doesn't remotely double your coverage of the possible-n-gram space once n is more than 2 or 3. Smoothing techniques (Laplace smoothing, backing off to shorter n-grams when a longer one wasn't seen) patch the zero-probability problem so the model doesn't outright fail, but they don't give the model any way to *generalize* — a smoothed n-gram model still has no notion that "the cat sat on the mat" and "the dog sat on the rug" are structurally similar sentences; it only knows literal counts of exact sequences it happened to see.

Neural language models fix this differently: they learn continuous embeddings where similar contexts land near each other, so the model can assign reasonable probability to a novel-but-plausible phrase it never saw during training, purely because it resembles something structurally similar it did see — that generalization capability is what counting-based methods structurally lack no matter how much data you throw at them.

**Testing:** whether you understand sparsity as a fundamental limitation of counting-based methods that more data can't fix, and can explain why neural approaches generalize where counting can't.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why n-gram sparsity isn't fixed by more data

interviewQuestions.question: Two teams report perplexity scores for their language models — 15 and 22 — and conclude the first model is clearly better. What would make you question that conclusion?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My first question would be whether both models use the exact same tokenizer and vocabulary, because perplexity is computed per token, and "what counts as one token" is entirely dependent on the tokenizer — comparing raw perplexity numbers across two different tokenizers is comparing numbers computed in different units, even though they look like the same kind of number. A model with a larger vocabulary that tends to represent common words as single whole tokens rather than splitting them into several subword pieces will systematically report lower perplexity per token, simply because each of its tokens carries more information on average — that's an artifact of the tokenization scheme, not evidence the model understands language better. A model using a smaller vocabulary with more aggressive subword splitting has to predict more, smaller tokens to cover the same text, and each individual token prediction is a somewhat easier, lower-information problem, which can inflate its measured perplexity relative to a model that isn't doing that.

So before accepting "model A (perplexity 15) beats model B (perplexity 22)," I'd verify: same tokenizer, same vocabulary size, evaluated on the exact same held-out text. If those don't match, the comparison is invalid on its face and needs to be normalized — for instance to a token-independent unit like bits-per-character, which measures information content in a way that doesn't depend on how the tokenizer happened to chop up the text. Only once the comparison is apples-to-apples does the "lower is better" conclusion actually hold.

**Testing:** whether you catch the tokenizer-mismatch pitfall specifically, rather than accepting a lower perplexity number as automatically meaning a better model.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Catching an invalid perplexity comparison
